title: William Whitley / Sportsman's Hill
summary: Near Crab Orchard, William Whitley finished Sportsman’s Hill in 1794, often called Kentucky’s first brick house, and raced horses on a clay oval beside it.
bodyMarkdown:
[William Whitley](https://grokipedia.com/page/william_whitley) came to Kentucky in 1775 as a young Virginian. He was born in 1749 to Ulster Presbyterian parents, and he arrived with his wife, [Esther Whitley](https://grokipedia.com/page/esther_whitley), whose own crossing is told in [Esther Whitley Over the Cumberlands, 1775](/stories/esther-whitley-over-the-cumberlands-1775/). The family lived first at St. Asaph's (Logan's Station) and at Fort Harrod before settling on their own land in what became [Lincoln County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lincoln_County,_Kentucky).

Whitley's reputation rested on frontier warfare. He served under George Rogers Clark, became a militia major in 1792, and in 1794 led a raid on a [Chickamauga Cherokee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Chickamauga_Cherokee) town. The Chickamauga were Cherokee who refused to accept land cessions and kept fighting settlement along the Cumberland and Tennessee rivers, and their raids and the settlers' reprisals fed each other for years (see [Chickamauga Cherokee](/stories/chickamauga-cherokee/)).

Whitley's home showed the same frontier logic. The brick house he and Esther built between 1787 and 1794 on a rise they called Sportsman's Hill is often described as the first brick house in Kentucky. It was also built for defense, with high windows and, according to the [state park description](https://eec.ky.gov/Nature-Preserves/Locations/Pages/William-Whitley-House.aspx), a hidden staircase and a hiding place above the kitchen.

Below the house Whitley laid out a circular racetrack of clay. Horses ran it counterclockwise, the reverse of the English custom of racing clockwise, and tradition remembers the choice as a pointed break from Britain. The [Kentucky Historical Society marker](https://history.ky.gov/markers/sportsmans-hill-2) dates the track to about 1780, while other local records put its laying out in 1788, when the Lincoln County Court ordered a road to the "race path." Racing on the course lasted until the Civil War.

Whitley died as he had lived. Past sixty, he volunteered for the War of 1812 and was killed on October 5, 1813, at the [Battle of the Thames](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_the_Thames) in Upper Canada. The same battle cost the life of the Shawnee leader [Tecumseh](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tecumseh). Some accounts credit Whitley with firing the fatal shot, but Richard M. Johnson is more often credited and the question remains unresolved.

## Kentucky today

The [William Whitley House State Historic Site](https://grokipedia.com/page/william_whitley_house_state_historic_site) preserves the brick house on Sportsman's Hill in Lincoln County. [Whitley County, Kentucky](https://grokipedia.com/page/william_whitley), and its county seat of Williamsburg were named for him in 1818, and a plaque on the county courthouse still credits him with the shot at the Thames.
